c2211adbe72a.title: Adapting Guidelines for Country use
c2211adbe72a.content: . The following page provides a reference to resources that can guide countries in adapting the specifications in this IG for country use. The specifications included in this implementation guide provides the generic, software agnostic and software neutral content requirements. They are documentation of generic system requirements that need to be adapted to local needs; and subsequently used to inform the design of digital systems implemented locally. WHO guidelines articulate and endorse rigorously tested recommendations for health interventions to be adopted within country programs. When applied correctly and consistently, guideline recommendations save lives. To ensure that countries can effectively benefit from digital health investments, the SMART Guidelines approach is intended to facilitate the adoption of WHO’s clinical, public health and data use guidelines in an accurate way in the digital systems that countries are adopting. For more on layers of knowledge representation and how they are used in WHO’s SMART Guidelines approach, see WHO’s SMART Guidelines and this Lancet article. Strategy and Investment . | Member States are increasingly looking to build or augment their own digital systems to protect their populations from climate-sensitive health threats; | Member States will further adapt and extend these specifications to suit their needs, moving from theoretical use cases to localized adaptation; | Member States have the capacity to maintain normative standards supported by consistent resourcing, ensuring the system evolves beyond initial project lifecycles. | . Infrastructure . | Member States must have access to reliable national epidemiological surveillance data and WMO-accredited climate data sources; | Member States possess or are in the process of developing a data integration layer that can ingest, transform, and unify data from both sources. | . Legislation, Policy and Compliance . | Member States must adhere to their national legal and policy frameworks when implementing a CHUD solution. | . Leadership and Governance . | A centralized infrastructure provides Member States the ability to enforce standards for data harmonization, ensuring different systems can “speak the same language”. | . Workforce . | Member States will ensure that surveillance officers, data publishers, and data analysts are trained to collaborate using the common language of the unified system. | . Services and Applications . | The CHUD solution operates as an ecosystem approach, connecting existing national surveillance systems and digital public infrastructure to enable early warning systems. Standards and Interoperability | For information related to standards and interoperability, see the Dependencies page. | . Edit this page on GitHub .

18312dedd641.content: . A business process, or process, is a set of related activities or tasks performed together to achieve the objectives of the health programme area, such as registration, counselling, referrals. Workflows are a visual representation of the progression of activities (tasks, events, interactions) that are performed within the business process. The workflow provides a “story” for the business process being diagrammed and is used to enhance communication and collaboration among users, stakeholders and engineers. The workflows included in this DAK depict processes that have been generalized across different contexts and may not reflect the variability and nuances across different settings. The simplicity of the workflow may not adequately illustrate the nonlinear steps that may occur. Overview of Key Business Processes . Process A: Provision of epidemiological data . Objective: Routinely collect, aggregate, and curate epidemiological data as part of the surveillance process, ensuring the timely provision of high-quality inputs for predictive modelling of dengue outbreaks. General note: Epidemiological data provision encompasses both aggregate surveillance reporting (routine counts for trends) and detailed case-based reporting (richer demographic and risk factor data for model calibration and “detective work”). While treated as a single process here, the system must handle both data granularities. Business process notes and annotations: . | Patient presents with dengue symptoms . | The epidemiological data collection and provision business process is triggered on the health system side by events where health system patients present with dengue symptoms and request clinical services. The patient is registered in the health system prior to the start of the clinical encounter. | Note: The "Patient registration" sub-process, coloured in purple, is not detailed in this first iteration of the business process. | . | Evaluate the patient against clinical case definition . | The healthcare worker performs an evaluation of the patient's symptoms against dengue clinical case definition, following the available clinical guidelines and guidance. | Guidelines: DENGUE Guidelines.pdf | . | Is the dengue clinical case definition met? . | The healthcare worker decides if the symptoms the patient presents meet the definition of a dengue case. In case the clinical case definition is not met, other relevant clinical services are offered (step 15). | . | Is a laboratory test required? . | The healthcare worker determines whether a laboratory test is required to confirm the suspected case, according to the national protocols. | In dengue-endemic countries laboratory confirmation is not necessary before notification but should be obtained. | Guidelines: DENGUE Guidelines.pdf | 2.3.1 A stepwise approach to the management of dengue (see Table 2.2) | . | Notify the case . | The healthcare worker reports the case to the facility surveillance team. The reporting should be automated, based on the data collected during the clinical encounter, and should be performed electronically through the electronic surveillance system. | At this point it is determined if the case is considered a suspected, probable or confirmed case | Early notification of dengue cases seen in primary and secondary care is crucial for identifying outbreaks and initiating an early response | "Passive surveillance" is the routine reporting of diseases, by which notification is usually initiated by health care providers. A particular challenge of passive surveillance systems is continuously to motivate health care providers to report cases in accordance with standardized case definitions. Unfortunately, in many dengue endemic countries, surveillance is only passive and relies on reports by local physicians who may not consider dengue in their differential diagnosis and/or fail to report cases quickly and routinely. As a result, an epidemic has often reached or passed its peak before it is recognized, and opportunities for control are missed. Designating dengue as a notifiable disease that is covered by public health legislation is one way to increase compliance with reporting | This step represents the generation of case-based epidemiological data. It captures detailed patient demographics and risk factors required for immediate outbreak investigation and high-resolution model calibration | Guidelines: DENGUE Guidelines.pdf | 2.3.1 A stepwise approach to the management of dengue (see Table 2.2) | . | Check the data quality . | The data reported by the healthcare workers are reviewed for accuracy, validity and completeness. | This can be supported through automated checks in a digital system. | . | Were data quality issues found? | Correct fixable data quality issues . | Where possible, inaccurate, invalid or incomplete data should be checked against source records and corrected according to the national standard operating procedures. | Depending on local policy, this step might need to be delegated to a person with the appropriate data access rights. | . | Generate facility-level reports . | The facility surveillance officer generates reports containing facility level data. | . | Submit facility-level data electronically . | This can be automated and done digitally. | Depending on the local policies and system design, an active "submission" may not be needed and the higher administrative levels (district, region, national authorities) should be able to access data directly in the system, for reporting purposes. | . | Compile and verify aggregate reports . | The surveillance officer, at a higher administrative level, generates aggregate reports of predefined indicators aligned with national dengue monitoring and evaluation guidelines. | Once generated, the reports are checked for any potential remaining data quality issues such as implausible values or outputs. | This can be automated and done digitally. | . | Were issues found in the reports? . | If so, the surveillance officer requests fixes for the issues (step 16). If no issues were identified, the flow continues with step 13 (Analyze and interpret the reports). | . | Analyze and interpret the reports . | The analyses and interpretation of the reports should identify opportunities to improve the performance of the health-care facility workers, such as tracing missing data or contacting patients who have not attended a clinic. | Data analysis and interpretation can be done regularly and should not be limited to the reporting schedule. | . | Submit data electronically . | This can be automated and done digitally. | Depending on the local policies and system design, an active "submission" may not be needed and the district-level, provincial-level and national-level ministry of health should be able to access data directly in the system, for reporting purposes. | . | Provide other relevant clinical services . | The health worker offers other relevant clinical and support services, including referrals, to the patient if dengue case definitions are not met. The services proposed are specific to each patient and clinical condition(s). | . | Request fixes . | In case the surveillance officer identifies issues in the reports, they request necessary fixes. | If the source of issues is represented by data quality, the fixes will be addressed at data collection level (step 8. Correct fixable data quality issues). | . | Provide feedback to the healthcare workers . | The surveillance officer or the surveillance team at the facility, district or national level will provide feedback to the healthcare workers who reported the data. The purpose of feedback is to reinforce health workers' efforts at participating in the surveillance system. Another purpose is to raise awareness about certain diseases and any achievements made by disease-control and prevention projects in the area. Feedback is classified as supportive when it reinforces and acknowledges good performance, and corrective, when a change in behaviour and improvement is required. | If data quality issues are identified, the facility may be required to restart the process and resubmit the data. | Guidelines and guidance: Integrated disease surveillance response in the WHO African region. Booklet four: sections 8 and 9 | 8.5.2 Feedback | . | Plan actions based on the feedback . | The facility surveillance officer reviews the feedback and formulates a targeted action plan to address identified issues or reinforce positive practices. | The plan may include corrective measures for data quality improvement, training needs, workflow adjustments, or reinforcement of successful practices. | . | Take actions based on the feedback . | Healthcare workers who submitted the data carry out the actions outlined in the action plan. | Implementation should be guided by the surveillance officer and may involve collaboration with other staff, adherence to updated procedures, or participation in follow-up activities. | . | . Process B: Provision of meteorological data/products . Objective: Collect meteorological observations and data necessary for dengue prediction models, curate the data and publish it on the WIS 2.0 network so that it can be retrieved by the data unification system, acting as a data consumer. General note: . The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Information System (WIS) is the global system through which WMO Members exchange meteorological, hydrological, and climate data in real-time or near-real-time. It ensures interoperability through standardized formats and a unified data catalogue. WIS (including WIS 2.0) enables observations, forecasts, and warnings to circulate seamlessly and consistently worldwide. | Real-time or near-real-time data is the range of data mandated for use with WIS2.0. Depending on the needs of the prediction model being used or developed and the data available through WIS2.0 in the specific context, this may require data storage by the model to achieve the desired data elements. Longer time ranges, such as historic data, may be accessible via WIS2.0; however, it is on a case-by-case basis. If historical data is required and not available via WIS2.0, this data should be sought from the nationally designated institutions or other authoritative data providers. Beyond the WMO climate and weather data exchange, international data centers such as [NCEI (Data Access | National Centers for Environmental Information)](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/search/index) and C3S (Climate Data Store), provide access to internationally exchanged data. If a denser spatial scale of the model or product is required – working directly with nationally designated institutions or other data providers for data access that is not real-time/near-real-time should be considered. | . Guidelines and guidance: . | Climate Data Management System Specifications. WMO-No. 1131 | Manual on the WMO Information System, Volume II – WMO Information System 2.0. Annex VII to the WMO Technical Regulations. WMO-No. 1060 | Guide to the WMO Information System, Volume II. WMO Information System 2.0. WMO-No. 1061 | . Business process notes and annotations: . | Publish meteorological data/products . | The Data Publisher publishes data and metadata to the Climate Data Management System (CDMS) to be stored, managed, and analysed. Data can include raw data or products. | Guideline: Climate Data Management System Specifications. WMO-No. 1131 | . | Quality control (QC) and validate data/products . | These data and metadata are curated, using pre-defined quality control methods and curation/editing tools, to ensure that the data content and formats are as expected. | . | Publish the discovery metadata . | The Data Publisher publishes to its WIS node the discovery metadata that describes the data it makes available and how those data can be accessed. It will further publish a notification message to its Message broker, announcing the availability of new data. | Discovery metadata must be published in the Global Discovery Catalogues before the data are published. | Guidelines: Manual on the WMO Information System, Volume II – WMO Information System 2.0. Annex VII to the WMO Technical Regulations. WMO-No. 1060 | Guide to the WMO Information System, Volume II. WMO Information System 2.0. WMO-No. 1061 | . | Validate and assess discovery metadata record . | The Global Discovery Catalogue will subscribe to notifications concerning the addition, updating, or deletion of discovery metadata records in the WIS centers. | On receipt of a notification about new or updated discovery metadata, the Global Discovery Catalogue will download and validate a copy of the discovery metadata record, against the WMO Core Metadata Profile 2 (WCMP2), before inserting the record into the catalogue. | Validation ensures compliance with the specification, while the assessment evaluates the discovery record against good practices. | The Global Discovery Catalogue will periodically assess discovery metadata provided by Data Publishers [National Centers (NCs) and Data Collection or Production Centers (DCPCs)] against a set of key performance indicators (KPIs) in support of continuous improvement. Suggestions for improvement will be reported to the Global Monitor against the centre identifier associated with the discovery metadata record. | Guidelines: Manual on the WMO Information System, Volume II – WMO Information System 2.0. Annex VII to the WMO Technical Regulations. WMO-No. 1060 | Guide to the WMO Information System, Volume II. WMO Information System 2.0. WMO-No. 1061 | . | Validation passed? | Publish data/products . | The data is published on the WIS2 Node. | The simplest way to publish data through WIS2 is to persist the data as files and publish those files on a web server. | The Data publisher might also provide interactive access to data with APIs, enabling patient applications to request only the data they need. | It is important to consider where the data are published. If the data relate to a specific country or territory, they should be published through a National Centre (NC). If they relate to a region, programme, or other specialized function within WMO, they should be published through a Data Collection or Production Centre (DCPC). | Guidelines: Guide to the WMO Information System, Volume II. WMO Information System 2.0. WMO-No. 1061 | . | Insert the discovery metadata in the catalogue . | The Global Discovery Catalogue ingests and publishes the valid discovery metadata records provided by Data Publishers. | The Global Discovery Catalogue may amend discovery metadata records to provide details on how to subscribe via Global Brokers to updates about the associated dataset. | Guidelines: Manual on the WMO Information System, Volume II – WMO Information System 2.0. Annex VII to the WMO Technical Regulations. WMO-No. 1060 | Guide to the WMO Information System, Volume II. WMO Information System 2.0. WMO-No. 1061 | . | Publish notification about new data/products . | The Global Broker republishes notifications from WIS nodes and Global Services, including notification messages advertising the availability of new data. | Guidelines: Guide to the WMO Information System, Volume II. WMO Information System 2.0. WMO-No. 1061 | . | Provide real-time or near-real-time data/products . | The Global Cache provides a highly available data server, from which a data consumer can download core data. As per clause 3.2.13 of the Manual on WIS, Volume II, data consumers should access core data from the Global Caches. | Upon receiving a notification message, the Global Cache downloads a copy of the data referenced in the message from the WIS2 Node, makes these data available on its server, and publishes a new notification message informing data consumers that they can now access these data on its server. | The Global Cache will subscribe to notification messages from other Global Caches, enabling it to download and republish data that it has not acquired directly from WIS2 Nodes. This ensures that each Global Cache holds data from every WIS2 Node. | Guidelines: Guide to the WMO Information System, Volume II. WMO Information System 2.0. WMO-No. 1061 | Manual on the WMO Information System, Volume II – WMO Information System 2.0. Annex VII to the WMO Technical Regulations. WMO-No. 1060 | . | Notify the Data Publisher . | The Global Discovery Catalogue will notify the data publisher if the discovery metadata record fails validation and provide recommendations for improvements. | Guidelines: Guide to the WMO Information System, Volume II. WMO Information System 2.0. WMO-No. 1061 | . | Fix discovery metadata . | The Data Publisher fixes the issues and re-publishes the discovery metadata record. | . | Request for direct access received? | Provide requested data/products . | A WIS node may restrict access to its core data, relying on Global Caches to provide access to data consumers. | Recommended data are never cached by the Global Caches, and may be provided by data publisher with conditions on use. This means that the data publisher may control access to recommended data. | If controlled access to the data has been implemented (for example, through the use of an API key), the download link should include a security object which provides the pertinent information (the access control mechanism used, where or how a data consumer needs to register to request access, and so forth). | Data publishers must ensure that core data that are not cached (republished on Global Cache) are publicly accessible from their WIS2 Node, that is, with no access control mechanisms in place. | Guidelines: Guide to the WMO Information System, Volume II. WMO Information System 2.0. WMO-No. 1061 | . | . Process C: Data unification . Objective: To receive or retrieve epidemiological and environmental data, perform quality assurance on the data, harmonize and unify the data so that it becomes ready for analysis and modelling. Business process notes and annotations: . | Define spatial and temporal parameters . | For epidemiological and entomological data, the type of data (real-time, historical, aggregate, case-based) required for model execution should be determined based on the model's specifications. This may influence the retrieval process and access methods. Please refer to model documentation for specific requirements. | For climate and weather data, the type of data required will depend on dengue prediction model being used or developed. To identify the appropriate data, the region/location, the spatial resolution (e.g. 25 km), the type and range (e.g. forecast range, hindcast range, reanalysis), and the update frequency (e.g. weekly) must be specified. These specifications enable the data analyst to understand which sources of data are required. | The epidemiological and entomological data and climate and weather data should match in spatial and temporal parameters for unification. | . | Subscribe to relevant WIS2 datasets . | 2.1 Find data/products in the WIS2 Global Discovery Catalogue: The first step to using data published via WIS2 is to determine which dataset or datasets contain the data that are needed. To do this, a data consumer, in our case the data unification system, may browse discovery metadata provided by the Global Discovery Catalogue. | A data consumer may discover a dataset using keywords, a geographic area of interest, temporal information, or free text. Matching search results from the Global Discovery Catalogue provide high-level information (title, description, keywords, spatiotemporal extents, data policy, licensing, contact information), from which data consumers can assess and evaluate their interest in accessing/downloading data associated with the dataset record. | 2.2 Find data/products via search engines: Internet search engines are able to index the discovery metadata in the Global Discovery Catalogue, thereby providing data consumers with an alternative means to search for WIS2 data. | 2.3 Subscribe to topics via WIS2 Global Broker: Data consumers requiring real-time notifications must subscribe to Global Brokers. Data consumers should subscribe to more than one Global Broker to ensure that notifications continue to be received if a Global Broker instance fails. | Data consumers should subscribe to notifications from a Global Broker, not to notifications directly from the Message Brokers operated by WIS2 Nodes. | WIS2 provides notifications about updates to datasets, for example, when a new observation record from an automatic weather station is added to a dataset of surface observations. These notifications are published on Message Brokers. Where data consumers need to use data rapidly once they have been published (for example, as inputs to a weather prediction model), they should subscribe to one or more Global Brokers to get notification messages using Message Queuing Telemetry Transport (MQTT) protocol. | Guidelines: Guide to the WMO Information System, Volume II. WMO Information System 2.0. WMO-No. 1061 | . | Retrieve meteorological data/products from WIS2 . | On receipt of a notification message, a data consumer needs to decide whether to download the newly available data. The content of the notification message provides the information needed to make this decision (see the Manual on WIS, Volume II – Appendix E. WIS2 Notification Message). | Once decided, the data unification system, playing the data consumer role, retrieves the meteorological data from: | Global Cache: The Global Caches are designed to help Members efficiently share real-time and near-real-time data. They ensure that core data are available to all on a free and unrestricted basis, as required by the WMO Unified Data Policy (Resolution 1 (Cg-Ext(2021))). | WIS2 Node: If frequent updates to a dataset are very large (for example, in the case of weather prediction models or remote sensing observations) data publishers will need to share the burden of distributing their data with Global Cache operators. Therefore, the data consumer might need to access the data directly from the Data publisher's WIS2 Node (with no access control mechanisms in place). | Recommended data, opposed to Core data, are not cached within WIS2 by the Global Caches, therefore are accessible directly on the WIS2 Node. Recommended data may be provided with conditions on use and/or subject to a license and may have access controls applied at the WIS2 Node. | Data archives are also usually accessed directly via the WIS2 Node, given that Global Caches provide only short-term data hosting (for instance, for 24 hours). | Guidelines: Guide to the WMO Information System, Volume II. WMO Information System 2.0. WMO-No. 1061 | Annex 1 of Resolution 1 (Cg Ext (2021)), the WMO Unified Policy for the International Exchange of Earth System Data, lists the core and recommended data to be exchanged for the following Earth system domains: weather, climate, hydrology, atmospheric composition, cryosphere, oceans, and space weather. WMO-No. 1281 | Manual on the WMO Information System, Volume II – WMO Information System 2.0. Annex VII to the WMO Technical Regulations. WMO-No. 1060 | . | Perform QA on the data . | The epidemiological and climate data retrieved by the data unification system undergoes quality control verifications. This might imply checking for data completeness, consistency and accuracy but also validating the data against data standards (FHIR for EPI data, WIS 2.0 for climate data). | The approach to data quality assurance will vary, with well-resourced nations increasingly leveraging automated processes for real-time consistency checks, while countries with emerging data systems may still rely on essential manual verification and communication with data providers to address complicated errors. | . | Parse the data . | The system parses the epidemiological and climate data/products retrieved from different sources to ensure the data is in the expected format. | . | Perform spatial and temporal harmonization . | This process acts as the bridge between the disparate data sources, aligning meteorological data (often gridded or point-based) and epidemiological data (aggregated by administrative boundaries) into a consistent framework; this is executed by a data analyst and/or the system depending on the infrastructure available (ranging from manual approaches to fully automated pipelines). | The data analyst and/or system performs temporal harmonization by converting high-frequency climate data (e.g., daily or hourly readings) into standard 7-day epidemiological weeks to match the health reporting cadence, applying configurable aggregation logic (e.g., mean, min, max) to accurately represent that week's conditions. | Spatial harmonization is achieved by mapping and aggregating data to the target administrative level (e.g., District), which involves handling resolution mismatches through techniques like downscaling coarse global forecast models (e.g., from 30 km to 2 km) or aggregating gridded data to fit district polygons. | To ensure robust modeling inputs, the workflow accounts for data discrepancies and uncertainties ensuring that the unified dataset compares "like with like". | . | Unify the data . | The system automatically unifies the two separate data streams (epidemiological and climate) into a unified repository making the data ready to be used in the prediction model(s). | . | . Additional considerations for adapting workflows . These workflows are meant to be generic and high-level. A degree of customization and adaptation will be needed as they are translated into a digital system for a specific context. The workflows are considered to be 80% complete – the other 20% will need to be done through a series of person-centered design methods and mechanisms to complete the workflows for implementation. For example, the approach to data quality assurance will need to be adapted to local capacities; while well-resourced nations may leverage automated processes for real-time consistency checks, countries with emerging data systems may still rely on essential manual verification and communication with data providers to address errors. Similarly, the level of automation in data unification will depend on the available infrastructure, ranging from fully automated pipelines to manual execution by a data analyst. Furthermore, local policies and system design will dictate specific workflow steps, such as whether facility-level data requires an active “submission” or if higher administrative levels (district, regional, national) can access data directly within the system. Finally, the specific predictive model selected for implementation will influence the retrieval process, determining whether real-time, historical, aggregate, or case-based data is required. 629811de7200.title: data-models-and-exchange
629811de7200.content: . This section contains the data models and data exchange protocols with actors and transactions defined. It is part of the L3 machine-readable knowledge representation. The pages included in this section are described below. | Actors - A list and description of software or human entities that interact with the system, derived from business requirements defined in the L2. | Sequence Diagrams - Sequence diagrams depicting the interactions between system actors, in order, derived from business processes in the L2. | Transactions - A defined list of system transactions at an atomic level for each actor along with narrative, capability statements, structure definition, questionnaires, document bundles and composition. It may also refer to transactions in other implementation guides. | Logical Models - A StructureDefinition resource that describes data element definitions and their associated rules of usage, derived from the data dictionary in the L2. | Indicators and Measures - A thematic list of indicators defined in the implementation guide that link to L1 and L2 guidance documents. | . Design Documentation -DRAFT- . The documentation below details how to use this IG to execute the decision logic and the resources required to do so including PlanDefinitions, ActivityDefinitions, ValueSets, and Libraries. PlanDefinitions . insert content here has been represented as a FHIR PlanDefinition conformant to the FHIR Clinical Practice Guidelines Implementation guide CPG-ComputablePlanDefinition. For example, there is a PlanDefinition for Hepatitis A, Measles, etc. The intention behind this design is for each implementation to utilize only the antigens that are required for their national/local context, as many countries have national vaccine routines, which may leverage the WHO guidance. The aim of this content was to be adaptable for those contexts. These PlanDefinitions can be found in the Artifact Index . ActivityDefinitions . To represent the activities that need to be carried out, this implementation guide follows the workflow patterns established by the base FHIR specification. Each antigen represented as a PlanDefinition will be processed to produce ActivityDefnitions conform to the FHIR Clinical Practice Guidelines Implementation guide CPG-ActivityProfiles. FHIR Library . The FHIR Library contains a base64 encoded CQL library which represents the decision logic as a series of boolean clauses. Each PlanDefinition and Measure will reference a Library from which each decision point can be made and specify which expression from the CQL is used to trigger a decision in PlanDefinition or where to retrieve data to create the MeasureReport in the Measure, repsectively. ValueSets . Many of the ValueSets used in this IG are from CPG on FHIR and the IPS. There are a number of generated ValueSets based on the user scenarios detailed in this IG. There is one exception to that format which is the vaccine libraries, which map the codes between a variety of different systems including SNOMED GPS and WHO ATC in order to allow implementers to search for any vaccine which might be applicable to their user. More details on this approach is provided below. Edit this page on GitHub .

cad64cc1052b.title: Data Dictionary
cad64cc1052b.content: . The data dictionary outlines the minimum set of data corresponding to different points of the workflow within the identified business processes. The data set can be used on any software system and lists the data elements relevant for service delivery and executing decision-support logic, and for populating indicators and performance metrics. 8a5edab28263.title: SMART DAK CHUD
8a5edab28263.content: . This SMART Guidelines L2 specifications and set of implementation tools are still undergoing development. Content is for demonstration purposes only. Introduction . Vector-borne diseases like dengue fever represent a significant and growing public health threat, heavily influenced by climate variability such as changes in temperature and rainfall. While public health officials recognize that outbreaks are intrinsically linked to these climate factors, they face a foundational challenge: epidemiological health data and meteorological climate data are locked in separate, fragmented systems that do not “speak the same language”. Prevention and preparedness require a portfolio of actions that bridge this divide. To transition from reactive response to proactive prevention, health systems must be able to anticipate outbreaks before they peak. This requires the integration of national surveillance data with reliable climate data to feed predictive models. However, this is not merely a technical challenge of moving data; it is a normative challenge of standardizing how disparate sectors collaborate. Purpose of this IG . This Implementation Guide (IG) lays out the business specifications for the Climate and Health Data Unification for Dengue Surveillance (CHUD) system. Its primary purpose is to define a clear, standards-based approach for integrating epidemiological and climate data to enable national and sub-national early warning systems. Rather than building new proprietary tools, this IG focuses on the “rules of the road” that allow existing investments, such as national surveillance systems and WMO climate services to interoperate effectively This document is software-agnostic and provides a starting point for Member States to design, develop, and deploy the data unification layer necessary for climate-informed health surveillance, leveraging Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) where available. Target audience . The primary target audience of this document comprises national authorities responsible for overseeing national disease surveillance and vector control programs, particularly those establishing data integration pipelines to build and calibrate dengue predictive models. It is also designed for National Meteorological Agencies and climate data publishers tasked with producing and publishing standardized climate data. Additionally, this document serves government partners- including academic institutions, international organizations, NGOs, and technical partners - supporting Member States in the development and deployment of CHUD solutions. Scope . In Scope . This IG specifically focuses on the data flow, standards, and harmonization processes that feed a district-level dengue prediction model. This document describes a specification for: . | Data Journey & Unification: Documenting the automated process of ingesting data from health surveillance systems and climate data sources (WIS 2.0) to a central point of unification. | Core Data Elements: Defining the minimum essential data required, specifically epidemiological counts and environmental factors such as total rainfall and mean air temperature in Celsius. | Harmonization Standards: Detailing the transformation of data to match temporally (converting daily climate data to epidemiological weeks) and spatially (aggregating climate data to district boundaries). | Interoperability Standards: Recommending open standards, specifically HL7 FHIR for health data exchange and WMO’s WIS 2.0 for climate data access. | . Out of Scope . Aspects that are considered out of the scope of this initial documentation are: . | Predictive Model Development: The mathematical development, algorithm selection, or calibration of predictive models. | Visualization Tools: Documenting specific software for reporting, dashboards, or decision support interfaces. | Entomological and other sources of data: While several sources of data are recognized as being also important for district-level modeling, such as mosquito indices and vector data, these have been excluded from this initial phase. | Clinical Protocols: The specific clinical care protocols for treating dengue patients once an outbreak is detected. | Considerations for monitoring and evaluation of CHUD roll-out and use. | . Assumptions . Meteorological data assumptions: . General Notes: . | The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) Information System (WIS) is the global system through which WMO Members exchange meteorological, hydrological, and climate data in real-time or near-real-time. It ensures interoperability through standardized formats and a unified data catalogue. WIS (including WIS 2.0) enables observations, forecasts, and warnings to circulate seamlessly and consistently worldwide. | Real-time or near-real-time data is the range of data mandated for use with WIS2.0. Depending on the needs of the prediction model being used or developed and the data available through WIS2.0 in the specific context, this may require data storage by the model to achieve the desired data elements. Longer time ranges, such as historic data, may be accessible via WIS2.0; however, it is on a case-by-case basis. If historical data is required and not available via WIS2.0, this data should be sought from the nationally designated institutions or other authoritative data providers. | Beyond the WMO climate and weather data exchange, international data centers such as NCEI (Data Access; National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI)) and C3S (Climate Data Store), provide access to internationally exchanged data. If the required data is not accessible via WIS2 or a denser spatial scale of the model or product is required – working directly with nationally designated institutions or other data providers for data access should be considered. | For this use-case, it is assumed that the required data for dengue prediction is accessible via WIS2.0 (or WIS2.0 Node). | . Epidemiological data assumptions: . | The definition of a week should include 7 days and should align with the same standards as used by the epidemiological indicators, known as the epidemiological week. | It is assumed that upstream data entering from health facilities contains manual entry errors (e.g., incorrect province names, misspellings). While basic validation is assumed at the source, the unification system acts on the assumption that a secondary automated cleaning phase is required to flag gross inconsistencies before harmonization. | . a0599017944a.title: Generic Personas
a0599017944a.content: . The CHUD solution operates at the national level. This national infrastructure enables the effective implementation of Climate-Informed Early Warning Systems, transforming raw surveillance and weather data into actionable district-level risk forecasts. A centralized approach facilitates the standardization of core data dictionaries and harmonization protocols, promoting interoperability between the Ministry of Health and National Meteorological Services. Targeted generic personas . The targeted personas for this CHUD DAK are stakeholders operating in settings where they manage meteorological data exchange or provide essential health interventions (specifically regarding Dengue surveillance and response). In this case, the Data Publisher, Data Collection or Production Center, Global Service Operator, and Global Information System Centers form the meteorological backbone, while the Healthcare Worker, Surveillance Officer, and Data Analyst form the health response layer. In the health systems surveyed for this DAK, the common combination of service providers involves the collaboration between meteorological technical staff (providing climate data) and public health officers (utilizing data for prediction). The key competences of these personas are defined by WMO technical regulations and WHO health workforce guidelines. The key competences of Health Service Manager and Healthcare worker are defined by WHO as follows (Table 3) (32). Table 3. Key settings . The CHUD solution operates at the intersection of meteorological data infrastructure and public health systems: . Meteorological Setting: WIS encompasses three types of centres. Global Information System Centres (GISCs) provide global connectivity and unified portals. Connected to these are Data Collection or Production Centres (DCPCs) responsible for regional data and forecast products. National Centres (NCs) operate on a national basis to distribute data to national users. Health Setting: Healthcare workers operate in clinical and community settings (primary care, hospitals) to identify Dengue cases. Surveillance Officers and Data Analysts typically operate at district, regional, or national public health offices, utilizing centralized infrastructure to generate insights. Digital services . It serves as the central repository where historical climate and health data are stored, cleaned, and made available for the analytics engine. | . | Health Management Information System (HMIS) | Stores routinely collected aggregate healthcare data and facilitates their analysis.
